 World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week 2026
 One Health, one action: Prevent AMR now
 18 November 2026 
 Statement 
 Reading time: 
 Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia 
 Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is 
one of the most pressing health and development challenges of our time, 
threatening our ability to treat common infections, deliver lifesaving medical 
care, ensure food security, and protect the effectiveness of medicines. 
Bacterial AMR is already associated with more than 4.7 million deaths annually. 
Without urgent action, AMR could cause up to 39 million deaths by 2050, and 
cost the global economy more than US$3.4 trillion annually, disproportionately 
affecting low- and middle-income countries. 
 This year, the theme of World AMR 
Awareness Week, “ One Health, one action: Prevent AMR now ,” reminds us 
that the health of people, animals, plants and the environment is deeply 
interconnected. Its message is simple: AMR is not a future threat, and action 
cannot wait. 
 There is strong global and regional 
momentum. The 2024 United Nations Political Declaration of the High-Level 
Meeting on Antimicrobial Resistance resolved to accelerate action. In the 
Region, Member States went further in 2025 by endorsing the Regional Roadmap 
to accelerate actions on antimicrobial resistance in the human health sector . 
The roadmap calls for updated and costed national action plans, stronger 
domestic ﬁnancing for AMR, comprehensive reporting of AMR and antimicrobial-use 
surveillance data, improved capacity for resistance testing, universal basic 
WASH services in health-care facilities, and stronger national infection 
prevention and control programmes. 
 These efforts are most effective 
when integrated into primary health care, universal health coverage, and 
broader work to build resilient health systems, instead of stand-alone 
programmes. The scale and pace of implementation must increase if the Region is 
to protect the health gains of recent decades and keep lifesaving 
antimicrobials effective for future generations. 
 As a One Health challenge, AMR requires sustained collaboration across human health, animal health, agrifood systems and the environment. Governments must lead this response, working with communities, health professionals, veterinarians, farmers, researchers, civil society, the private sector and development partners.
 Working with the Quadripartite Collaboration for One Health—alongside FAO, UNEP and WOAH—and other partners, WHO will continue to advance the One Health approach through improved surveillance and early warning systems, integrated risk assessment, stronger laboratory networks, workforce development, and coordinated emergency preparedness and response.
On World AMR Awareness Week, WHO calls on all stakeholders to move from awareness to action. We call on Member States to accelerate implementation of commitments, invest in prevention, strengthen surveillance and laboratory capacity, and safeguard antimicrobials through responsible use and effective stewardship. We reaffirm our commitment to a sustained, collective effort, so that progress in one sector reinforces progress in all others. Together we can build a healthier, safer, and more sustainable future for everyone.
